note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Interpret an assessment question's steer and keywords before writing

evidence.title: Question analysis sheet read through the academic literacies lens
evidence.example: You take one essay question and mark up its steer (the instruction word) and its keywords, then write two sentences on what each asks you to do. Using Lea and Street (1998), you note that knowing what a tutor means by a steer is part of academic socialisation into a subject, not a fixed rule (for example, what "assess" asks for in a geography question on flood management). This shows you can interpret a question before you start writing.
evidence.artefact: A marked-up assessment question with the steer and keywords labelled and a short note on what each asks for.

evidence.title: Annotated brief for your first marked assignment
evidence.example: Before starting your first marked assignment, you annotate the brief: the steer, the keywords, the word count and the marking criteria. You then check your reading with your tutor or at a writing support drop-in (for example, a first-year nursing reflection that asks you to "discuss" a care episode, not describe it). This shows you read a brief to find out what is being asked before you begin.
evidence.artefact: The annotated assignment brief with a dated note of the tutor's or adviser's confirmation of your reading.
grounding: professional: Reads a brief to establish what is being asked, by whom and against what criteria before starting work.

genericOutcomes.title: Form analysis matched to a task's instruction
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how a task's steer and keywords indicate the form of writing it requires, before drafting begins.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a set task and identify the form it expects, such as an argument, a report or an analysis, by reading its steer and keywords closely rather than guessing from habit. You set out what producing that form well would involve before you begin drafting. A recognised account of writing development treats this kind of noticing as part of learning what a field expects writing to look like. This shows you can read a task's instruction to work out the form it requires.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note identifying the required form from a task's steer and keywords, written before drafting began.

genericOutcomes.title: Brief read to identify the required output
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify, from an instruction's wording, the form, audience and standard a piece of writing must meet before starting to write.
genericOutcomes.example: Given an instruction to produce a piece of writing, you work out before starting what form it needs to take, who will read it and what standard it will be judged against, rather than beginning with whatever format feels familiar. You note this down and check it against the original instruction once a first section is drafted. This shows you can read an instruction accurately enough to produce the form that is actually required.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note setting out the required form and audience, checked against the instruction once drafting began.
grounding: professional: Reads a brief to establish what is being asked, by whom and against what criteria before starting work.

capabilities.statement: Follow the writing cycle to plan and complete a first draft

evidence.title: Writing process log mapped to the writing cycle
evidence.example: You keep a short log while you write one essay, recording what you did at each stage of the writing cycle and labelling it with Flower and Hayes' (1981) planning, translating and reviewing. Using Lea and Street (1998), you add a note on which conventions you were still learning (for example, how to open a 1,000-word sociology essay). This shows you followed a set method from plan to a complete first draft.
evidence.artefact: A one-page process log with dated entries for each stage of the writing cycle, attached to your plan and first draft.
grounding: model: Cognitive process theory of writing (Flower and Hayes 1981)

evidence.title: Society end-of-year report planned and drafted
evidence.example: As a committee member of a student society, you are asked to write the end-of-year report for the students' union. You make a plan of headings first, write a full rough draft in one sitting, and only then tidy it (for example, a film society report covering screenings, membership and spending). This shows you can plan a document and get a complete first draft down before polishing.
evidence.artefact: Your dated plan, the unpolished first draft and the final submitted report, kept together as one portfolio page.
grounding: professional: Plans a document and gets a full working draft down before polishing it.

genericOutcomes.title: Staged draft built to match a required form
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can describe planning, drafting and reviewing as distinct stages needed to produce a complete first draft in a required form.
genericOutcomes.example: You use a staged process, plan first, then draft, then review, to produce a complete first version of a piece of writing in the form a task requires, rather than starting on finished sentences. At the planning stage you set out how the required form shapes your structure; only once a full draft exists do you check it against that form closely. A recognised model of how writers work treats planning and drafting as separate stages. This shows you can follow a writing cycle to reach a complete first draft.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A plan, a complete first draft and a short note on how the draft matches the required form.

genericOutcomes.title: Working draft completed before refining the form
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can plan a structure and produce a complete working draft of a document before refining it to match its required form.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task to produce a piece of writing in a particular form, you plan its structure first, then write a complete working draft before adjusting it to fit that form more precisely. You resist the urge to perfect the opening paragraph before the rest exists, since a full draft shows whether the structure actually works. This shows you can follow a staged process to produce a first complete draft in the form required, ready for focused revision.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated plan and a complete first draft, annotated to show where it was adjusted to fit the required form.
grounding: professional: Plans a document and gets a full working draft down before polishing it.

capabilities.statement: Find and correct errors in own writing by proofreading and editing

evidence.title: Two-pass error log separating editing from proofreading
evidence.example: You review one of your drafts in two separate passes: an editing pass for meaning and order, then a proofreading pass for surface errors such as comma splices. Using Lea and Street (1998), you note that error-spotting alone matches their study skills model, and that editing also asks what your subject expects (for example, a psychology lab report). This shows you can find and correct errors in your own writing.
evidence.artefact: A marked-up draft with an error log sorting each correction into editing or proofreading, with the type of error named.

evidence.title: Proofread volunteer handbook update for a food bank
evidence.example: Volunteering at a local food bank, you are asked to check an updated volunteer handbook before it is printed. You read it once for sense and once for errors, keep to the organisation's style, and send back a list of corrections (for example, inconsistent opening times and a run-on sentence in the safety section). This shows you can check and correct a document before it goes out.
evidence.artefact: The tracked-changes copy of the handbook and a short email from the coordinator confirming the corrections were used.
grounding: professional: Checks and corrects documents before they go out.

genericOutcomes.title: Error review checked against a form's requirements
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can distinguish correcting surface errors from checking a draft's structure against the form its writing is required to take.
genericOutcomes.example: Reviewing a completed piece of writing, you separate correcting surface errors, spelling, punctuation and slips, from checking that the piece still follows the structure its form requires. You treat these as different kinds of check, since a sentence can be grammatically correct yet still fail to do what that form needs. A recognised account of writing development supports treating these as distinct skills rather than one general check. This shows you can proofread and edit with an eye on the form a piece of writing is meant to take.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A marked-up draft with corrections split into surface errors and structural changes, noting the form required.

genericOutcomes.title: Final check against required form before sending
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can proofread and edit a finished document, correcting surface errors and confirming it follows the structure its form requires.
genericOutcomes.example: Before a finished document goes to its reader, you check it twice: once for surface errors such as typing slips and once to confirm it still follows the structure and style that this type of document requires. You correct anything that falls short rather than letting familiarity with the text stop you from seeing its errors. This shows you can proofread and edit a document so it is both free of errors and in the form it is actually expected to take.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The corrected document with a short list of surface and structural fixes made before it was sent.
grounding: professional: Checks and corrects documents before they go out.

capabilities.statement: Identify and structure the essay and other argued genres

evidence.title: Genre map comparing an essay and a problem question
evidence.example: You compare two argued genres in your subject and map how each is structured, using Swales' (1990) idea that a genre belongs to a discourse community with shared purposes. With Lea and Street (1998), you explain why tutors expect each structure (for example, a law essay that argues a position versus a problem question that applies the law to facts). You then choose and justify the structure for your own assignment.
evidence.artefact: A side-by-side structural map of two genres, annotated, with a paragraph justifying the structure used in your own assignment.
grounding: model: Genre analysis and discourse community (Swales 1990)

evidence.title: Choosing the right document type on a placement
evidence.example: On a placement in a software team, you are asked to make the case for changing a testing process. You decide whether a briefing note, report or proposal suits the reader, explain your choice and structure the document to fit it (for example, a two-page proposal for a team lead with a costed option). This shows you can identify an argued genre and structure it for its purpose.
evidence.artefact: The finished document with a short written rationale for the genre chosen and your supervisor's feedback on it.
grounding: professional: Chooses and follows the right document type (briefing, report, case note, proposal) for the reader and purpose.

genericOutcomes.title: Argued form selected to match a task's purpose
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse a task to identify which argued form it calls for and explain how that form's structure differs from others.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task that calls for an argued piece of writing, you work out which form it actually requires, a sustained argument, a structured response to a problem, or something else, and identify how its expected structure differs from the others. You set out the sections or stages each form would need before choosing one and building your own piece around it. This shows you can identify the argued form a task requires and structure writing to match it, rather than applying one structure to every task.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short comparison of two argued forms with a structure plan for the one chosen for the task.

genericOutcomes.title: Right argued format matched to its reader
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can select the argued form a task requires and structure a piece of writing so each part fulfils that form's purpose.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task that needs an argued case made to a particular reader, you decide which format that argument should take and structure it so each part does the job that format requires, rather than writing everything as flowing prose regardless of purpose. You check the finished piece against what that format is normally expected to contain before treating it as complete. This shows you can identify and produce the argued form of writing a task actually calls for.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The finished document checked against the sections or stages its chosen format is expected to contain.
grounding: professional: Chooses and follows the right document type (briefing, report, case note, proposal) for the reader and purpose.

capabilities.statement: Write clear sentences in the active voice

evidence.title: Sentence rewrite commentary on active and passive voice
evidence.example: You take a paragraph of your own and rewrite it in subject, verb, object order, changing passive sentences to active ones where that makes them clearer. Using Lea and Street (1998), you judge where the passive is a disciplinary convention and where it only hides who did what (for example, a chemistry method versus the discussion section). This shows you construct clear sentences and choose voice deliberately.
evidence.artefact: A before-and-after paragraph with a commentary explaining each change and each passive sentence you chose to keep.

evidence.title: Plain English customer email template at work
evidence.example: In a part-time job in a customer contact centre, you rewrite a standard email that customers often misread. You shorten sentences, put the person doing the action first and cut jargon, then ask colleagues to test it (for example, a refund email that now says "We will refund you within five days"). This shows you write plain, active English a busy reader understands first time.
evidence.artefact: The old and new email templates side by side with notes on each change and your manager's approval.
grounding: professional: Writes in plain, active English that a busy reader understands first time.

genericOutcomes.title: Sentence clarity checked against a form's expectations
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse sentence construction to judge when active voice better serves a piece of writing's required form and reader.
genericOutcomes.example: Reviewing a piece of writing meant to be read quickly and acted on, you check each sentence for subject, verb and object order, and rewrite any that bury the main action in a long clause or hide who is responsible for it. You judge voice choice against what that form requires to be useful to its reader, rather than treating every passive sentence as automatically wrong. This shows you can write clear, active sentences suited to the form a piece of writing needs to take.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A rewritten extract with a short note on which sentences were changed to active voice and why.

genericOutcomes.title: Active sentences rewritten for a quick reader
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can rewrite passive sentences into clear, active ones so a reader can follow a document's point without delay.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a document meant to be read quickly and acted on, you check each sentence for length and clarity, rewriting passive constructions into active ones so the person responsible for an action is always named near the start of the sentence. You test the result by timing how long it takes someone unfamiliar with it to understand the main point. This shows you can write clear, active sentences that let a busy reader understand a document in the form it actually requires, the first time.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The rewritten document with timing notes from a reader test and a short list of sentences changed.
grounding: professional: Writes in plain, active English that a busy reader understands first time.

capabilities.statement: Use the four pillars to review and structure own writing

evidence.title: Reverse outline review using the four pillars
evidence.example: You use the guide's four pillars of effective writing as a self-review lens on a full essay draft. You reverse outline it, checking that each paragraph has a topic sentence and one point, and restructure where it does not. Using Lea and Street (1998), you note which choices follow your subject's expectations (for example, an education essay on inclusive classroom practice). This shows you evaluate and restructure your own writing.
evidence.artefact: A reverse outline of your draft before and after revision, with notes against each pillar on what you changed.

evidence.title: Restructured report for a museum live brief
evidence.example: On a live brief for a local museum, you write a report on visitor feedback. You plan it so each section and paragraph makes one point, then move the recommendations to the front because the client reads those first (for example, a history module project on a new gallery trail). You explain how this differs from an essay that builds to its conclusion. This shows you can organise writing so a reader can follow it.
evidence.artefact: The client report with a short note on its structure and the museum contact's written response to it.
grounding: professional: Organises a document so that each section and paragraph makes one point the reader can follow.

genericOutcomes.title: Draft restructured to fit its required form
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate a draft's structure against the form it is required to take and identify where it must be reorganised.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a complete draft and check it section by section against the structure that its particular form is expected to follow, moving or cutting any paragraph that does not hold to one clear point. Where the expected structure differs from how you first organised the piece, you note why and restructure accordingly rather than leaving the mismatch in place. This shows you can review and restructure your own writing so it actually takes the form that kind of writing is required to take.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A before-and-after structure map of a draft with notes on each change made to fit its required form.

genericOutcomes.title: Document restructured to suit its reader and form
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can restructure a draft document so its sections match what its required form is expected to deliver to its reader.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a finished draft of a document, you check whether its structure matches what that type of document is expected to deliver, then reorder or rewrite sections so each one makes a single point a reader can follow quickly. Where the form calls for conclusions or recommendations near the start rather than the end, you move them, explaining the change in a short note. This shows you can structure a piece of writing to fit the form a task actually requires, not just the order ideas occurred to you.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The restructured document with a short note explaining each change made to match its required form.
grounding: professional: Organises a document so that each section and paragraph makes one point the reader can follow.

capabilities.statement: Recognise how writing conventions vary by discipline

evidence.title: Comparative analysis of writing conventions across three disciplines
evidence.example: You collect three published extracts from different disciplines and analyse their conventions: voice, use of evidence, structure and hedging. Using Lea and Street's (1998) academic literacies model, you argue that these differences reflect each discipline's ways of making knowledge, not right or wrong styles (for example, as a joint honours biology and philosophy student comparing a results section with an argued paper). You then apply your findings to your own writing.
evidence.artefact: A comparative table of conventions across three annotated extracts, with a commentary on how you adapted your own writing.
grounding: model: Genre analysis and discourse community (Swales 1990)

evidence.title: Technical and public versions of the same findings
evidence.example: On a placement with an environmental consultancy, you write up a habitat survey in the firm's technical format, then adapt it for a community consultation. You decide what to keep, what to explain and what to drop for each audience (for example, turning species tables into a plain summary of what the development means locally). This shows you write in a profession's conventions and adapt them for readers outside it.
evidence.artefact: The paired technical and public documents with a reflective note on the conventions you changed, signed by your supervisor.
grounding: professional: Writes in the conventions of one's profession and adapts them for readers outside it.

genericOutcomes.title: Required form identified across differing conventions
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique how writing conventions vary across disciplines and justify which convention a given form of writing actually requires.
genericOutcomes.example: You compare how two fields expect a similar kind of claim to be written up, noticing that one favours tentative, hedged statements while the other states findings directly, and you work out what each convention is trying to achieve for its readers. You then identify which convention the form you are writing in actually requires, rather than assuming your usual style will transfer unchanged. This shows you can recognise that writing conventions vary and use that recognition to produce the form a particular piece of writing requires.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short comparison of two sets of conventions with a note on which one the task at hand requires.

genericOutcomes.title: Writing style adjusted to match required conventions
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify the conventions a disciplinary context expects and adapt their own writing to construct a piece that meets them.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task that needs writing up in a form you are less familiar with, you identify its expected conventions, how direct or hedged its claims should be, how evidence is normally presented, before drafting, rather than writing in your usual style and hoping it transfers. You check a finished section against those conventions and adjust anything that does not fit. This shows you can recognise that writing conventions differ across contexts and adapt your own writing to match the one a task actually requires.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A drafted section checked against the expected conventions of its required form, with adjustments noted.
grounding: professional: Writes in the conventions of one's profession and adapts them for readers outside it.

capabilities.statement: Integrate sources actively, own point first

evidence.title: Voice audit of literature review paragraphs
evidence.example: You audit three paragraphs of your literature review, highlighting your own claims and the sources in different colours. Drawing on Lea and Street's (1998) attention to authority and identity in student writing, you rewrite paragraphs led by sources so each opens with your point, uses paraphrase, and uses sources to support or qualify it (for example, a criminology review on desistance). This shows you integrate sources actively with your own point first.
evidence.artefact: Colour-coded before-and-after paragraphs with a commentary on how your voice and the sources' voices now relate.

evidence.title: Evidence-led recommendation paper for a sports club
evidence.example: Working with a university sports club, you write a short paper recommending a change to how coaches monitor training load. You lead with your recommendation, then cite the research and the club's own data that support or qualify it (for example, injury records set against two sport science studies). This shows you can put your own point first and use evidence to back it in a real setting.
evidence.artefact: The recommendation paper with its reference list and the head coach's written response, showing whether the change was adopted.
grounding: professional: Leads with one's own recommendation and cites the evidence that supports or qualifies it.

genericOutcomes.title: Sources selected and ranked to support one point
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify the selection and ranking of sources by their relevance to a position, ensuring the writer's own point leads the argument.
genericOutcomes.example: Having gathered several sources on a question, you select only those relevant to the point you intend to make, set aside the rest, and rank the ones kept by how directly they support or complicate your position. You then draft a paragraph that states your point first and brings in the strongest source as support, rather than summarising every source you found in turn. This shows you can find, select and use sources appropriate to a task while keeping your own point in charge of the writing.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short list of sources ranked by relevance, with a paragraph showing your point stated before the sources.

genericOutcomes.title: Relevant sources selected to support a recommendation
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can select sources relevant to a recommendation and construct a response that states their own judgement before citing supporting evidence.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a question to answer with evidence, you search out several possible sources, then select only the ones that are actually relevant to the recommendation you intend to make, discarding sources that are merely related to the topic. You draft your recommendation first and attach the selected sources as support rather than letting whatever you found first dictate your conclusion. This shows you can find, select and use appropriate sources while keeping your own judgement at the front of the writing.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The recommendation with its supporting sources listed, each one noted as directly relevant to the point made.
grounding: professional: Leads with one's own recommendation and cites the evidence that supports or qualifies it.

evidence.title: Writer's positioning statement for a master's dissertation
evidence.example: You write a reflective statement on how you position yourself as an author in your dissertation, using Ivanic's (1998) distinction between the autobiographical self, the discoursal self and the self as author, and Lea and Street's (1998) academic literacies model (for example, a public health dissertation where you write as a former practitioner). You show how your choices of voice and evidence fit, or knowingly depart from, your discipline's conventions.
evidence.artefact: A 1,000-word positioning statement with excerpts from your dissertation annotated to show deliberate authorial choices.

evidence.title: Writing portfolio for specialist and non-specialist readers
evidence.example: On an industry-sponsored engineering project, you write for three readers: a technical report for the sponsor, a lay summary for site staff and a short conference abstract. You then reflect on how your writing moved between these communities and what each demanded of you (for example, how much uncertainty to state for each reader). This shows you write with awareness of your discipline and its wider context.
evidence.artefact: A portfolio of the three pieces with a reflective commentary on your disciplinary writing choices and the sponsor's feedback.

genericOutcomes.title: Form chosen to fit a field's expectations
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique how a field's conventions shape the form expected of its writing and justify choices that depart from or follow them.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a task that could reasonably be written several ways, you work out which form your field expects for this kind of claim and reflect on why that form suits the kind of knowledge the field builds, rather than treating the choice as arbitrary. You note where you choose to follow that expectation and where you deliberately depart from it, giving a reason either way. This shows you can write with awareness of how your field shapes the form a piece of writing is expected to take.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reflective note explaining the form chosen for a piece of writing and the reasoning behind it.

genericOutcomes.title: Writing choices explained for a wider readership
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a document that serves specialist and non-specialist readers, justifying which disciplinary conventions to keep, explain or drop.
genericOutcomes.example: Asked to produce a piece of writing that specialists and non-specialists will both read, you decide, section by section, which conventions of your field to keep, which to explain and which to drop, and you can explain the reasoning behind each decision if asked. You check a finished draft against both kinds of reader before treating it as complete. This shows you can write with awareness of your field's conventions while still producing a form that a wider readership can follow.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A finished document checked against both specialist and non-specialist readers, with reasons for key choices noted.
grounding: professional: Adapts the same substantive content for specialist and non-specialist readers.
